thread.title: Sketching a plan for the Triad as a cybersecurity hub

author: John Joyce
title: Sketching a plan for the Triad as a cybersecurity hub
text: – Reporter, Triad Business Journal Nov 6, 2018, 6:45am EST Patrons inside The Coffee Mill, a small java shop in Lewisville, probably didn't take notice Monday of the man in the red shirt at the checkerboard table in the corner. Nor should they. It's the kind of place where folks come to read or chat with other coffee lovers, where the menu is scribbled in chalk and the barista is decked out in a white on white button down shirt and black vest. Besides, there is nothing to belie from Rob Arnold's appearance that he sometimes testifies before Congress , attends meetings in Washington, D.C. with Cabinet members and top representatives from McAfee Inc. (NYSE: MFE), Apple Inc. (NYSE:AAPL), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and others . Yet Arnold is quickly becoming an expert voice in the national conversation on cybersecurity – all this from a quiet launch in 2015 out of a small Winston-Salem incubator space at Flywheel co-working space . Arnold and his partners at Threat Sketch, a cybersecurity startup with two government contracts through the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, are keen to take their company's model for protecting nonprofits and small government entities from the threat of cyberattacks and making the same protections available to – and affordable for – small businesses. Most cybersecurity firms are aiming at Fortune 500 with the most money to spread around, Arnold said. "Granted, there is a lot of money, but there are a little over six million small businesses that are not just a shell company, not defunct, that are true employer businesses with revenue and so forth," he said. That's were Threat Sketch aims to make its hay: taking what for those giant companies is six-figure threat assessment and offering it to small- to mid-sized businesses for $1,000. First things first, however. Today marks the soft launch of the company's first endeavor with Homeland Security, shoring up nonprofits' defenses against the threat of outside attacks. Immediately following the full launch, after a few rounds of testing and assessments, Threat Sketch will employ its same model to protecting small government bodies. Arnold illustrated the Threat Sketch model by quoting Henry Ford: "Sell to the classes, eat with the masses. Sell to the masses, eat with the classes." Threat Sketch already has demonstrated rapid growth, outgrowing its Flywheel space and taking up a second location inside the Winston Starts incubator recently launched in Winston-Salem . From there, Arnold hopes to grow larger still and occupy dedicated space and employ more than the 23 full-time, part-time and contracted employees on staff. "As one of our early investors pointed out, we are exceptionally well positioned, timing wise. Everybody kind of wants to be in cybersecurity now," he said. Shading in the details Threat Sketch takes an asset profile of the entity it is working with, breaking down the 10 to 12 categories of potential cyber risk. It then overlays cybercrime statistics on top of that, Arnold said. "We use very high level threat categories. We use things like denial of service, viruses, malware, crimeware, ransomeware, phishing attacks," he said. From there, Threat Sketch works with the company's CEO, IT crowd, even the sales and marketing team to put in place prevention and preparedness steps regarding a potential attack. The model works across all three target sectors Threat Sketch has marked out for its projected growth: nonprofit, small government and small commercial business. Within a few years, Arnold expects to either be acquired or profitable enough not to need to be. "We assume that’s going to happen, but if it didn’t it is going to still be such a cash cow that – because our kind of back-of-the-napkin pro formas – could easily exceed $100 million in terminal revenue value in a relatively short period of time," he said. A Triad cyber-hub Arnold's ambition for his efforts in cybersecurity step outside of his own company. He intends to help build a framework for a center for cybersecurity in the Triad that will be on par with what the Research Triangle Park in Raleigh is for pharmaceuticals or what Durham is known for in software development. He hopes to align with other cybersecurity firms, with cyber attorneys and IT professionals, and also insurance agents and agencies dealing in cyber protections, to build a network that brings the Triad to the forefront nationally in cyberthreat prevention and protection. "We are representing the region," Arnold said. "I’d really like us to find some way to come together and build a center of excellence within the Piedmont Triad." The framework is there, he said. "I feel like I’ve made enough inroads at the national level that I can help coalesce and help make those kind of things happen, but I can’t do it alone," he said.
